I feel that others can see what happened to me just by looking at me

vignette: Farid was twenty-eight when the city he called home fractured. He remembers the morning the sirens stopped and the ground began to shudder, the way the air turned thick with the smell of displaced dirt and crushed limestone. He and his neighbors had huddled in the basement of a crumbling apartment block for eleven days. He recalls the specific rhythm of the shells—how they cracked the air like heavy boards snapping, how the dust settled in his throat and on his tongue, tasting of dry earth. He remembers hearing the name of their neighborhood leader, Yasser, called out over the static before the radio went dead. That night, the world narrowed to the weight of silence, the taste of soil, and the sudden, sharp sounds that preceded every collapse. Those acoustic patterns, that particular grit in the air, and those specific voices became the architecture of his survival. When Farid returned to the United States, he carried the weight of those eleven days in his shoulders. The first winter, he stopped walking through community parks. The smell of damp mulch after a spring rain made his chest tighten, so he began taking the same back routes to the grocery store, keeping his head down, breathing through his mouth to avoid the scent of outdoor earth. At the dance studio where he teaches and choreographs, he found himself stepping back during drills. A dropped mat or a sudden clap of hands sent his pulse racing. Over the next several months, he quietly asked his colleagues to use electronic metronomes instead. He told his wife, Lina, that he preferred the digital click, but what he meant was that the live sounds felt too much like the basement walls giving way. He stopped answering calls from old acquaintances. When he heard a familiar accent or a name like Yasser spoken in passing, he would abruptly change the subject or leave the room. He described it to his sister simply as feeling dead inside, a hollow space behind his ribs where his reactions used to be. He stopped attending Friday prayers and stopped returning his neighbors’ greetings. He had come to believe that people were fundamentally unreliable, that trust was a luxury the world had already stripped from him. In the rehearsal studio, surrounded by mirrored walls, he felt acutely exposed. He was certain that everyone could see what happened to him just by looking at him, that the tension in his jaw or the stillness of his eyes gave away the war. He began wearing high collars and long sleeves even in summer. His posture remained guarded during critiques, and the studio’s hardwood floors, usually resonant under his soles, now felt like a stage where he could not hide. These habits accumulated over the last eighteen months. His choreography grew more rigid, his partnerships fractured when he withdrew from physical contact, and his marriage strained under the quiet distance he maintained. He finally walked into the clinic because his feet, usually reliable partners in his craft, had begun to ache during warm-ups he could no longer tolerate. He wanted to know how to walk through a park without his breath catching, how to hear his own name spoken in a crowded room without bracing for impact, and how to stop feeling like a ghost in his own life. What frightened him most was not the memories themselves, but the certainty that he would always be this way—permanently severed from the present, waiting for the ground to shake again.
